agent.name: Agent
agent.short: An LLM-powered system that takes multiple steps toward a goal — calling tools, observing results, and deciding what to do next — rather than producing a single response.
agent.def: An agent is an LLM wrapped in a loop: it reads the current situation, decides on an action (often a tool call like running a command or querying an API), observes the result, and repeats until the task is done or it gives up. Agents exist because many real tasks — fixing a bug, booking a trip, researching a question — can't be done in one shot; they require acting on the world and reacting to what comes back. This loop structure is exactly what makes agents hard to evaluate: there are many paths to success, failures compound across steps, and the same agent can succeed one run and fail the next. See What Makes Agents Different.

trajectory.name: Trajectory
trajectory.short: The full step-by-step record of an agent run: every model response, tool call, and result from start to finish.
trajectory.def: A trajectory is the complete sequence of everything an agent did during one run: each reasoning step, each tool call, each result that came back, in order. It is the agent-world equivalent of a trace, and it matters because an agent's final answer alone tells you almost nothing about why it succeeded or failed — the interesting information (wrong tool, bad plan, recovered from an error) lives in the steps. Evaluating agents usually means either scoring the end result (outcome-based) or scoring the trajectory itself (process-based).

tool-call.name: Tool call
tool-call.short: A single action an agent takes on the outside world — running a shell command, calling an API, querying a database — requested by the model and executed by the harness.
tool-call.def: A tool call is the mechanism by which an LLM acts instead of just talking: the model emits a structured request ("run ls", "search the web for X", "update row 12"), the surrounding program executes it, and the result is fed back into the model's context. Tool calls are what turn a text generator into an agent. For evaluation, they are both the unit you inspect when reading a trajectory (did it call the right tool with the right arguments?) and a major source of failure modes — agents can pick the wrong tool, malform the arguments, or misread the result.

environment.name: Environment
environment.short: The simulated or real world an agent acts in during an eval — a codebase, a website, a computer desktop, a database — that responds to the agent's actions.
environment.def: The environment is everything the agent can act on and observe: a Git repository it can edit, a browser it can click around in, an operating system, a mock airline-booking database. Agent benchmarks differ from ordinary question-answering benchmarks chiefly in that they must ship an environment, not just questions — and the environment's fidelity and graders determine what the score actually means. A buggy or too-forgiving environment quietly measures the wrong thing. See The Agentic Benchmark Landscape for how major benchmarks build theirs.

outcome-based-evaluation.name: Outcome-based evaluation
outcome-based-evaluation.short: Grading an agent only on whether the end result is correct, ignoring how it got there.
outcome-based-evaluation.def: Outcome-based evaluation scores an agent by checking the final result — do the tests pass, is the right row in the database, did the user get a correct answer — without judging the steps taken. Its appeal is objectivity: a passing test suite is a passing test suite, no judge required. Its blind spot is everything in between: an agent can reach the right outcome through reckless or destructive intermediate steps, or fail at the last moment after a nearly perfect run, and outcome grading sees only pass or fail. Most serious agent evals pair it with process-based inspection of trajectories.

process-based-evaluation.name: Process-based evaluation
process-based-evaluation.short: Grading an agent on the quality of its steps — the trajectory — not just the final result.
process-based-evaluation.def: Process-based evaluation looks inside the run: did the agent make a sensible plan, call appropriate tools, avoid forbidden actions, recover from errors? It exists because outcomes alone can mislead — a correct answer reached by luck or by a dangerous shortcut is not the same as a correct answer reached well, and a near-miss failure contains diagnostic gold that a 0/1 outcome score throws away. The cost is subjectivity: judging a trajectory usually requires a rubric and often an LLM judge, which brings its own biases. See What Makes Agents Different.

user-simulation.name: User simulation
user-simulation.short: Using an LLM to play the human user in a multi-turn agent eval, so conversations can be run automatically at scale.
user-simulation.def: Many agent tasks involve a back-and-forth with a person ("I want to change my flight" … "which flight?" … "the Tuesday one"). User simulation replaces that person with another LLM, prompted with the user's goal and persona, so thousands of conversations can run unattended. This is what lets benchmarks like tau-bench evaluate conversational agents at all — but it adds a second model whose own mistakes (revealing too much, misunderstanding, going off-script) get tangled into the agent's score. See Reliability: pass^k and Repeated Trials.

pass-hat-k.name: pass^k
pass-hat-k.short: The probability that an agent succeeds on ALL k independent attempts at the same task — a reliability metric. Contrast with pass@k, where any one success counts.
pass-hat-k.def: pass^k ("pass-hat-k") asks: if you run the same task k times, what fraction of tasks does the agent get right every single time? It is the metric tau-bench introduced for measuring reliability, and it is the mirror image of pass@k, which counts a task as solved if any of k attempts succeeds. The distinction matters because deployment cares about consistency: a customer-service agent that succeeds on a task half the time looks fine under pass@k but is unusable, and pass^k makes that visible — it falls fast as k grows unless the agent is genuinely consistent. See Reliability: pass^k and Repeated Trials.

state-based-evaluation.name: State-based evaluation
state-based-evaluation.short: Grading an agent by comparing the final state of its environment (e.g. a database) against the known goal state, regardless of the path taken.
state-based-evaluation.def: State-based evaluation checks the world, not the words: after the agent finishes, the harness compares the environment's final state — database rows, files on disk, a calendar — to the goal state the task defines. If the task was "cancel the Tuesday flight," the grader just checks whether the booking record now says cancelled. This sidesteps judging conversation quality or step choices entirely, which makes it cheap and objective, and it naturally allows multiple valid paths to the same goal. Its limits are the flip side: it can't tell a graceful run from a chaotic one, and it only works when the goal state can be specified precisely. See Reliability: pass^k and Repeated Trials.

sandbox.name: Sandbox
sandbox.short: An isolated, disposable execution environment (often a container or VM) where an agent can run code and modify files without affecting anything real.
sandbox.def: A sandbox is a walled-off copy of the world — typically a Docker container or virtual machine — where the agent can execute commands, edit files, and break things freely. Evals need sandboxes for two reasons: safety (agents run arbitrary model-generated code, which you do not want touching your real machine) and reproducibility (every run starts from the same clean snapshot, so results are comparable across runs and across models). Harnesses like Inspect build sandbox management in as a first-class feature.

scaffold.name: Scaffold
scaffold.short: The program structure around a model — prompts, tools, retries, control flow — that turns a raw LLM into a working agent. Different scaffolds give the same model very different scores.
scaffold.def: A scaffold is everything you wrap around the model to make it function as an agent: the system prompt, the set of tools it can call, the loop that feeds results back, retry logic, stopping rules. The same model under different scaffolds can perform wildly differently, which creates a chronic evaluation problem: when a leaderboard entry beats another, is the model better or just the scaffold? Careful benchmark reporting separates the two (e.g. SWE-bench results are properly read as model-plus-scaffold results). See Case Study: SWE-bench and Cost Frontiers and Time Horizons.

elicitation.name: Elicitation
elicitation.short: The effort spent getting a model's best possible performance — better prompts, tools, scaffolding — before measuring it. Low elicitation makes a capable model look weak.
elicitation.def: Elicitation (a term used heavily in the METR evaluation methodology) is the work of drawing out what a model can actually do before you score it: tuning prompts, fixing tool bugs, adjusting the scaffold, giving it a fair number of attempts. It matters because an eval is supposed to measure the model's capability, but what it directly measures is model-plus-setup — and a sloppy setup produces a false negative about capability. This cuts both ways: for safety-motivated evals, under-elicitation is the dangerous error, because "the model couldn't do it" might really mean "we didn't try hard enough." See Cost Frontiers and Time Horizons.

time-horizon.name: Time horizon
time-horizon.short: A way of expressing agent capability as the length of human task (in human time-to-complete) the agent can finish reliably — e.g. 'tasks that take a person an hour.'
time-horizon.def: A time horizon measures agent capability on a human-meaningful scale: instead of "scored X% on benchmark Y," it says "can complete tasks that take a skilled human about this long." The idea, from the METR time-horizon work, is to make capability comparable across very different tasks and trackable over time — task length in human hours is a single axis on which both a five-minute lookup and a multi-day engineering project sit. The reliability threshold matters enormously: the length of task an agent finishes half the time is very different from one it finishes almost always. See Cost Frontiers and Time Horizons.

cost-controlled-evaluation.name: Cost-controlled evaluation
cost-controlled-evaluation.short: Comparing agents at equal cost (dollars or tokens), not just on accuracy — because rerunning an agent many times buys accuracy that says nothing about the model.
cost-controlled-evaluation.def: Cost-controlled evaluation reports accuracy together with what it cost to achieve, and compares systems at comparable spend. The argument, made forcefully in the "AI Agents That Matter" critique, is that agent accuracy is purchasable: wrap any model in enough retries and ensembling and its score rises, so a leaderboard sorted by accuracy alone rewards burning money rather than building better agents. Plotting accuracy against cost and looking at the Pareto frontier shows which systems are genuinely better and which are just more expensive.

pareto-frontier.name: Pareto frontier
pareto-frontier.short: On an accuracy-vs-cost plot, the set of systems that no other system beats on both axes at once — the only ones worth choosing.
pareto-frontier.def: When you plot eval results on two axes — say accuracy versus cost — a system is Pareto-optimal if nothing else is both more accurate and cheaper. The Pareto frontier is the curve through those undominated points, and everything below or right of it is strictly worse than some available alternative. The concept (borrowed from economics) matters for evals because single-number leaderboards hide trade-offs: the "best" agent by accuracy may be dominated in practice by one that gets nearly there at a fraction of the cost. See Cost Frontiers and Time Horizons.

holdout-set.name: Holdout set
holdout-set.short: A portion of eval data kept aside and never used during development, so it can give an honest score that iteration hasn't quietly optimized toward.
holdout-set.def: A holdout set is data you deliberately don't look at while building: you iterate on prompts, scaffolds, and graders against one slice of your eval, then measure the finished system once on the held-out slice. The reason is a quiet failure mode: every time you tweak your system to fix failures you saw, you fit it a little more to those specific cases — and the dev-set score drifts upward without the underlying system getting better on anything else. The holdout score is the honest one precisely because nothing was tuned against it. Note that a holdout you re-check after every change stops being a holdout. See From Failure Modes to Evals.

overfitting.name: Overfitting
overfitting.short: When a system (or your prompt/scaffold tuning) gets good at the specific examples it was developed against, without getting better at the general task they represent.
overfitting.def: Overfitting is fitting the quirks of your data rather than the pattern it samples: a model, prompt, or agent scaffold tuned until it aces a particular set of test cases may have learned those cases, not the task. In eval work this bites twice — models can overfit public benchmarks (everyone optimizes toward the same famous test sets), and you can overfit your own eval by iterating against it until the score is meaningless. The standard defense in both cases is the same: keep a holdout you don't iterate against, and refresh test data periodically. See Data Contamination for the training-data version of this problem.

random-variable.name: Random variable
random-variable.short: A quantity whose value depends on chance — like 'whether this eval sample passes' or 'this run's score.' The basic object probability theory works with.
random-variable.def: A random variable is a number determined by a chance process: the result of a die roll, or — closer to home — whether a given eval sample passes (1) or fails (0) when you run it. The concept exists so we can reason precisely about uncertain quantities: once "this sample's outcome" is a random variable, we can talk about its average behavior (expectation), its spread (variance), and how those propagate into the uncertainty of a whole benchmark score. Eval scores are built out of many small random variables, which is why statistics applies to them at all. Gentle introduction in Appendix A.

expectation.name: Expectation
expectation.short: The long-run average value of a random quantity — what you'd get if you could repeat the experiment forever and average the results.
expectation.def: The expectation (or expected value, or mean) of a random variable is its probability-weighted average: the value its average converges to over infinitely many repetitions. For evals it is the quantity you actually care about but can never observe directly — a model's "true" pass rate on a task distribution is an expectation, and the score from any finite eval run is just an estimate of it. Almost all of eval statistics is about how far that estimate might sit from the expectation it is estimating. See Appendix A.

variance.name: Variance
variance.short: A measure of how spread out a random quantity is around its average — high variance means individual results land far from the mean.
variance.def: Variance measures spread: it is the expected squared distance between a random variable and its mean. A high-variance eval score bounces around a lot from run to run; a low-variance one is stable. The squaring is a mathematical convenience (it makes variances of independent things add up nicely), but it puts the number in awkward squared units — which is why in practice you usually take its square root, the standard deviation, to get back to interpretable units. Variance is the raw ingredient behind every error bar in this course. See Appendix A.

standard-deviation.name: Standard deviation
standard-deviation.short: The square root of variance: the typical distance between an individual observation and the average, in the same units as the data.
standard-deviation.def: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, restoring the units of the original quantity: if scores are percentages, the standard deviation is in percentage points. Read it as "roughly how far a typical single observation sits from the mean." Keep it distinct from the standard error, which measures uncertainty in an average of many observations — the standard deviation describes the data's spread and doesn't shrink as you collect more, while the standard error shrinks with sample size. See Appendix A.

standard-error.name: Standard error
standard-error.short: How much an estimate (like a benchmark score) would typically vary if you reran the whole measurement — the basic unit of an error bar.
standard-error.def: The standard error answers: if I could repeat this entire eval with a fresh sample of tasks, how much would the resulting score typically move? It is the standard deviation of the estimate rather than of individual data points, and it shrinks as the sample grows — averaging more tasks cancels out more of the per-task luck. This single number is what separates "Model A scored two points higher" from "Model A scored two points higher, but the scores wobble by three points run to run, so this means nothing." It is the foundation of error bars on eval scores; the mechanics live in Appendix B.
standard-error.also: SEM, standard error of the mean

central-limit-theorem.name: Central limit theorem
central-limit-theorem.short: The result that averages of many independent measurements follow a predictable bell-curve pattern, regardless of what the individual measurements look like.
central-limit-theorem.def: The central limit theorem (CLT) says that when you average many independent random quantities, the average itself follows an approximately normal (bell-curve) distribution — even if each individual quantity is as un-bell-like as a 0/1 pass-fail outcome. This is the load-bearing wall under eval statistics: it is why a benchmark score (an average of many per-sample results) has predictable uncertainty, and why the simple formulas for standard errors and confidence intervals work for pass rates. The approximation needs enough samples and reasonable independence between them. See Appendix B.

confidence-interval.name: Confidence interval
confidence-interval.short: A range around an estimate (e.g. 'score 72%, give or take 3') built so that the procedure captures the true value most of the time across repeated experiments.
confidence-interval.def: A confidence interval turns a point estimate plus its standard error into a range: "the measured pass rate is 72%, and the plausible range for the true pass rate is roughly 69–75%." The careful interpretation is about the procedure: a 95% interval is constructed by a recipe that brackets the truth in 95% of repeated experiments — it is not a 95% probability statement about this one interval, though the practical reading ("values in this range are consistent with the data") serves well. For evals, the headline use is overlap: when two models' intervals heavily overlap, the data may not distinguish them. See Error Bars on Eval Scores and Appendix B.

clustered-standard-errors.name: Clustered standard errors
clustered-standard-errors.short: A standard-error correction for when eval samples come in related groups (e.g. several questions about the same document), which makes naive error bars too small.
clustered-standard-errors.def: Standard error formulas assume each sample contributes independent information. But eval datasets often have clusters — several questions drawn from the same document, several turns from the same conversation, several tasks from the same repository — and samples within a cluster tend to succeed or fail together. Treating them as independent overcounts your evidence and produces error bars that are too narrow, making noise look like signal. Clustered standard errors fix this by computing variability at the cluster level rather than the sample level. See Error Bars on Eval Scores and Appendix F.

paired-comparison.name: Paired comparison
paired-comparison.short: Comparing two models on the same questions and analyzing the per-question differences — which cancels question difficulty and detects smaller gaps with the same data.
paired-comparison.def: A paired comparison runs Model A and Model B on the identical set of samples and looks at the difference per sample, instead of comparing two overall averages. The point is noise cancellation: much of an eval score's variability comes from which questions happen to be hard, and since both models face exactly the same questions, that shared difficulty subtracts out of the differences. The result is a far more sensitive test — gaps that are statistically invisible when you compare unpaired averages become clearly detectable when paired. This is the single highest-leverage statistical trick in comparing two models; mechanics in Appendix C.

hypothesis-test.name: Hypothesis test
hypothesis-test.short: A formal procedure for asking whether an observed difference (e.g. between two models' scores) is too large to be plausibly explained by random noise.
hypothesis-test.def: A hypothesis test starts from a skeptical default — the null hypothesis, usually "there is no real difference" — and asks how surprising the observed data would be if that default were true. If the data would be very surprising under "no difference" (a small p-value), you treat the difference as real. The procedure exists because eval scores are noisy and humans are eager: without a discipline for distinguishing signal from luck, every two-point wiggle becomes a press release. See Comparing Two Models and Appendix C.

null-hypothesis.name: Null hypothesis
null-hypothesis.short: The skeptical default assumption in a hypothesis test — typically 'these two models are actually equally good and the observed gap is just noise.'
null-hypothesis.def: The null hypothesis is the boring explanation a hypothesis test tries to rule out: no real difference, no real effect, the observed gap is sampling luck. Tests are built around it because "prove there's a difference" is hard but "show the data would be very unlikely if there were none" is tractable — you can compute exactly how much wiggle pure noise produces and check whether the observed gap exceeds it. Failing to reject the null is not proof the models are equal; it just means the data couldn't tell them apart, which is often a sample-size problem. See Appendix C.

p-value.name: p-value
p-value.short: The probability of seeing a difference at least as large as the one observed if there were really no difference at all. Small p-value = hard to explain as noise.
p-value.def: A p-value answers one specific question: if the null hypothesis were true (no real difference), how often would random noise alone produce a gap this big or bigger? A small p-value means "noise rarely does this," which is evidence the difference is real. It is famously misread: a p-value is not the probability the null is true, and "statistically significant" is not the same as "large" or "important" — with enough samples, trivially small differences become significant. Pair it with the effect size to judge whether a real difference also matters. See Appendix C.

statistical-power.name: Statistical power
statistical-power.short: The probability your test will detect a real difference of a given size if one exists. Low power means real improvements look like 'no significant difference.'
statistical-power.def: Statistical power is the chance that your experiment finds an effect that is genuinely there. An underpowered eval — too few samples for the size of difference you care about — will routinely report "no significant difference" between models that really do differ, and worse, the differences it does flag will tend to be flukes that happened to be exaggerated. Power is what you buy with sample size and with variance-reducing designs like paired comparisons; planning it before running the eval is how you avoid spending compute on an experiment that couldn't have answered your question. See Appendix C.

type-i-error.name: Type I error
type-i-error.short: A false alarm: concluding there's a real difference when there isn't one — the noise fooled you.
type-i-error.def: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it was actually true: declaring Model B better than Model A when the gap was pure sampling luck. The conventional significance threshold is essentially a cap on how often you're willing to make this mistake. The eval-specific trap is multiplicity: if you compare many models, many subsets, or re-test after every tweak, each look is another chance for a false alarm, and "we found a significant improvement" becomes nearly guaranteed by sheer volume of looking. See Appendix C.

type-ii-error.name: Type II error
type-ii-error.short: A miss: failing to detect a difference that really exists — usually because the sample was too small for the size of the effect.
type-ii-error.def: A Type II error is the opposite failure to a false alarm: the difference between models was real, but your test didn't have the resolution to see it, so you concluded "no significant difference." Its probability is one minus the test's statistical power. In eval practice this error is quietly common — small eval sets simply cannot detect modest improvements, so teams discard genuinely better prompts or models because the eval shrugged. The fix is more samples, paired designs, or honestly reporting "inconclusive" rather than "no difference." See Appendix C.

pass-at-k.name: pass@k
pass-at-k.short: The probability that at least one of k independent attempts at a task succeeds. The standard metric for code generation, where one working solution is all you need.
pass-at-k.def: pass@k measures: given k tries at a problem, what's the chance at least one succeeds? It fits settings where a single success is all that matters — code generation, where you can run the tests and keep the attempt that passes. It was popularized by the HumanEval benchmark, which also introduced the now-standard unbiased estimator for it: naively running exactly k samples gives a noisy, biased estimate, so instead you generate more than k and compute the combinatorial formula. Don't confuse it with pass^k, which requires all k attempts to succeed and measures reliability rather than best-case ability. See pass@k Done Right.

unbiased-estimator.name: Unbiased estimator
unbiased-estimator.short: A way of estimating a quantity from data whose errors average out to zero — it's right on average, even though any single estimate may be off.
unbiased-estimator.def: An estimator is any recipe for guessing a true quantity from a finite sample; it is unbiased if, averaged over many repetitions of the experiment, its guesses center exactly on the truth — no systematic lean high or low. Unbiasedness matters in evals because biased estimators corrupt comparisons in a way more data doesn't fix: the famous example is the naive pass@k computation, which systematically misestimates, versus the combinatorial estimator from the HumanEval work, which is provably unbiased. Note an unbiased estimator can still be noisy; bias and variance are separate problems. Derivation in Appendix D.

bootstrap.name: Bootstrap
bootstrap.short: Estimating uncertainty by resampling your own data with replacement many times and seeing how much the statistic of interest varies across resamples.
bootstrap.def: The bootstrap answers "how much would my number wobble if I reran the experiment?" without rerunning anything: you draw many fake datasets by sampling your real data with replacement (the same sample can appear multiple times), recompute your statistic on each, and read the spread of the results as your uncertainty. Its appeal for evals is generality — it works for awkward statistics like medians, win rates, or judge-aggregated scores where no tidy standard-error formula exists, and it adapts naturally to clustered data by resampling whole clusters. The cost is compute and care with dependence structure. See Appendix F.

binomial-distribution.name: Binomial distribution
binomial-distribution.short: The probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent yes/no trials — the natural model for 'how many of my 200 eval samples pass.'
binomial-distribution.def: The binomial distribution describes the count of successes in n independent pass/fail trials that each succeed with the same probability. It is the default statistical model for an eval score: if a model truly passes each task with some probability, the number of passes in your test set is binomial, and everything else — the standard error of a pass rate, why error bars shrink with more samples, the wobble you see between runs — follows from its math. The independence assumption is the part that breaks in practice (see clustered standard errors). Gentle treatment in Appendix A.

bernoulli-trial.name: Bernoulli trial
bernoulli-trial.short: A single chance event with exactly two outcomes (success/failure) — the statistical model of one eval sample passing or failing.
bernoulli-trial.def: A Bernoulli trial is the simplest random variable there is: one event, two outcomes, success with some probability p. It is the atom of eval statistics — "does this sample pass?" is a Bernoulli trial, and a benchmark score is just the average of hundreds of them. The reason the term earns a name at all is composability: stack n independent Bernoulli trials and you get the binomial distribution, from which standard errors, confidence intervals, and pass@k all flow. See Appendix A.

spearman-correlation.name: Spearman correlation
spearman-correlation.short: A measure of how well two rankings agree — used, e.g., to check whether an LLM judge ranks outputs in the same order humans do.
spearman-correlation.def: Spearman correlation measures agreement between two rankings: convert each set of scores to ranks (best, second-best, …) and ask how similar the orderings are, from perfect agreement through no relationship to perfectly reversed. It exists because raw score agreement is often the wrong question — a judge whose scores run systematically high but sort outputs in the right order is still useful for picking winners, and Spearman captures exactly that while ignoring the offset. In eval work it shows up when validating judges against humans and when comparing one leaderboard's ordering to another's. See Appendix E.

cohens-kappa.name: Cohen's kappa
cohens-kappa.short: An agreement score between two raters that subtracts out the agreement they'd get by random chance — raw percent-agreement flatters easy labeling tasks.
cohens-kappa.def: Cohen's kappa measures how often two raters (two humans, or a human and an LLM judge) give the same label, corrected for chance. The correction is the whole point: if most outputs pass, two raters who label nearly everything "pass" will show high raw agreement while contributing almost no real judgment — kappa asks how much better than that baseline coincidence the agreement actually is. It is a standard tool for checking judge-human alignment and inter-annotator agreement before trusting labels. See Appendix E.

confusion-matrix.name: Confusion matrix
confusion-matrix.short: A 2×2 table counting a classifier's (or judge's) hits and misses: true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives.
confusion-matrix.def: A confusion matrix tabulates predictions against truth: how many real positives were caught (true positives), how many were missed (false negatives), how many negatives were correctly left alone (true negatives), and how many were falsely flagged (false positives). It exists because a single accuracy number hides which kind of mistake dominates — and the two kinds usually have very different costs. In eval work the "classifier" is often an LLM judge being checked against human labels: the matrix shows whether it tends to wave bad outputs through or fail good ones, which a headline agreement rate can't. Nearly every metric in Appendix E — precision, recall, TPR, TNR, F1 — is read off this table.

precision.name: Precision
precision.short: Of everything the system flagged as positive, what fraction actually was? High precision means few false alarms.
precision.def: Precision answers: when the classifier (or judge, or guardrail) says "positive," how often is it right? It is computed from the confusion matrix as true positives divided by all predicted positives. It matters whenever acting on a flag is costly — a hallucination detector with low precision drowns reviewers in false alarms until they stop reading it. Precision says nothing about what was missed; that is recall's job, and the two trade off against each other, which is why they are always reported together. See Appendix E.

recall.name: Recall
recall.short: Of all the actual positives out there, what fraction did the system catch? High recall means few misses.
recall.def: Recall answers: of everything that truly was positive, how much did the classifier find? From the confusion matrix: true positives divided by all actual positives. It is the metric to watch when misses are expensive — a safety guardrail with low recall lets real harms through no matter how clean its alerts look. Recall is trivially gamed in isolation (flag everything and you catch everything), which is exactly why it is paired with precision; the same quantity under the name true positive rate or sensitivity appears in judge-alignment work. See Appendix E.

true-positive-rate.name: True positive rate (TPR)
true-positive-rate.short: The fraction of actual positives correctly identified — same quantity as recall. In judge validation: of the outputs a human passed, what share did the judge also pass?
true-positive-rate.def: The true positive rate (TPR) is the proportion of genuine positives the system correctly labels positive — mathematically identical to recall, but the TPR/TNR framing is the one used when validating LLM judges against human experts: treating the human label as truth, TPR asks "of the outputs the human passed, what fraction did the judge pass too?" Reporting TPR and TNR as a pair reveals a judge's directional lean — lenient judges show high TPR but low TNR — which a single overall agreement number conceals. See Appendix E.

true-negative-rate.name: True negative rate (TNR)
true-negative-rate.short: The fraction of actual negatives correctly identified. In judge validation: of the outputs a human failed, what share did the judge also fail?
true-negative-rate.def: The true negative rate (TNR) is the proportion of genuine negatives the system correctly labels negative. In judge validation it is usually the harder, more telling half of the TPR/TNR pair: most LLM judges lean lenient, so they sail through the "agree on good outputs" test (high TPR) while waving through outputs the human expert rejected (low TNR). Since catching bad outputs is typically the whole reason the judge exists, a low TNR can disqualify a judge that looks fine on overall agreement. See Appendix E.

f1-score.name: F1 score
f1-score.short: A single number combining precision and recall (their harmonic mean), high only when both are high — a convenient but lossy summary.
f1-score.def: The F1 score compresses precision and recall into one number using the harmonic mean, which punishes imbalance: a system great at one and poor at the other scores closer to its weak side than a simple average would. It exists because leaderboards and dashboards want one number per system. Use it knowing what it hides — F1 weighs false alarms and misses equally, and in most real applications they are not equally costly, so when the trade-off matters, report precision and recall separately. See Appendix E.

sample-size.name: Sample size
sample-size.short: The number of test cases in your eval. It directly controls how small a real difference you can reliably detect — and the cost of more resolution grows fast.
sample-size.def: Sample size — the number of eval cases, usually written n — is the main lever on statistical resolution: error bars shrink proportionally to the square root of n, so quadrupling your dataset only halves the noise. This square-root law explains a lot of eval practice: why tiny eval sets can only detect huge differences, why detecting a small improvement needs a disproportionately large set, and why paired comparisons (which cancel noise instead of out-massing it) are so valuable. Planning n from the size of difference you care about, rather than from whatever data was lying around, is the discipline called power analysis. See Appendix B and Appendix C.

effect-size.name: Effect size
effect-size.short: How big a difference actually is (e.g. five percentage points), as opposed to whether it's statistically detectable. Significance without size can be meaningless.
effect-size.def: Effect size is the magnitude of a difference in real terms — Model B passes five percentage points more tasks than Model A — kept deliberately separate from whether the difference is statistically significant. The separation matters because significance is a function of both size and sample size: with enough samples, a difference too small to matter to any user becomes "significant," and with too few, a difference big enough to change your model choice doesn't register. Good eval reporting gives both: the size of the gap, and the uncertainty around it. See Appendix C.

independence.name: Independence
independence.short: The assumption that one sample's outcome tells you nothing about another's. Most eval statistics quietly depend on it, and grouped or related samples violate it.
independence.def: Two random outcomes are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Nearly every formula in basic eval statistics — standard errors, confidence intervals, the binomial model of a pass rate — assumes your samples are independent, and the assumption fails quietly: ten questions about the same document, multiple turns from one conversation, or several tasks in one repository tend to succeed or fail together. Correlated samples carry less information than their count suggests, so naive error bars come out too narrow and noise masquerades as signal. The fixes are clustered standard errors or cluster-aware resampling. See Appendix B.

contamination.name: Contamination
contamination.short: When a benchmark's test data ended up in a model's training data, so the model may have memorized answers — and the score measures memory, not ability.
contamination.def: Data contamination happens when the questions (or answers) of a benchmark appear in the data a model was trained on. LLMs train on enormous web scrapes, and popular benchmarks are all over the web — in papers, blog posts, GitHub repos, tutorial sites — so contamination is the default condition for any public test set, not an exotic accident. A contaminated score is invalid in a specific way: it measures the model's ability to recall this particular test, which says nothing about performance on new problems. Detecting it (fresh parallel questions, n-gram overlap, log-likelihood probes) and defending against it (live benchmarks, private holdouts, canary strings) are whole subfields.
contamination.also: data contamination, benchmark contamination, train-test contamination

memorization.name: Memorization
memorization.short: A model reproducing specific content it saw during training (like a benchmark answer) rather than solving the problem — the mechanism behind contamination.
memorization.def: Memorization is when a model's output comes from recalling training data rather than from generalizable skill. LLMs genuinely do store and reproduce specific sequences they trained on, especially ones repeated often in the data — and famous benchmark problems are repeated very often. This is the mechanism that makes contamination ruinous: a model that memorized a benchmark's answers performs like an expert on those exact items and like its true self everywhere else. Telltale signs include acing a famous test while flunking lightly reworded versions of the same problems.

construct-validity.name: Construct validity
construct-validity.short: Whether a test actually measures the ability it claims to measure — e.g. whether a coding benchmark score really reflects coding skill.
construct-validity.def: Construct validity asks: does this measurement measure the thing it claims to? The "construct" is the abstract ability you care about — coding skill, factual accuracy, agentic competence — and the benchmark is just a proxy for it, built from specific tasks, graders, and assumptions. Validity breaks whenever the proxy can be satisfied without the ability (weak tests that pass wrong solutions, answers leaked in the prompt, memorized solutions) or the ability fails the proxy (formatting trips up a capable model). The term comes from psychometrics, the field that has spent a century learning how hard it is to measure abilities through tests. It is the central concept of What Does a Score Mean?.

internal-validity.name: Internal validity
internal-validity.short: Whether an eval's results are correct on their own terms — the grading is right, the harness isn't buggy, the comparison is apples-to-apples.
internal-validity.def: Internal validity is about the integrity of the measurement itself: were the answers graded correctly, did the harness run what you think it ran, were both models given the same inputs under the same conditions? An eval can fail internally in mundane ways — a parsing bug that marks correct answers wrong, tests too weak to catch incorrect solutions, different prompt formats for different models — and these errors corrupt the score before any deeper question of meaning arises. Internal validity is the precondition for external validity: a measurement must first be right before it can generalize.

external-validity.name: External validity
external-validity.short: Whether eval results generalize beyond the test itself — does scoring well on the benchmark predict performing well on real tasks in the wild?
external-validity.def: External validity asks whether results transfer: a model aces a benchmark of self-contained Python puzzles, but does that predict anything about its performance on your team's sprawling legacy codebase? Every benchmark makes simplifications — curated tasks, clean environments, unambiguous grading — and external validity is the question of how much those simplifications cost when you extrapolate to messier reality. It is why high benchmark scores routinely coexist with disappointing real-world performance, and why evals built from your own product's failures beat generic benchmarks for product decisions. See What Does a Score Mean?.

data-leakage.name: Data leakage
data-leakage.short: Any path by which information a system shouldn't have at test time reaches it anyway — training on test data, answers visible in inputs, hints in the setup.
data-leakage.def: Data leakage is the umbrella term for information sneaking across a boundary it shouldn't cross, inflating measured performance. In LLM evals it shows up in several forms: test data in the training set (contamination), answers embedded in the task input itself (solution leakage), future information available to an agent that wouldn't exist in the real scenario, or dev-set knowledge bleeding into a supposedly held-out test. The common thread: the system passes the test using a side channel rather than the ability being measured, so the score overstates what it will do when the channel is absent.

solution-leakage.name: Solution leakage
solution-leakage.short: When a benchmark task's input accidentally contains its own answer — e.g. a GitHub issue that spells out exactly what code fix to make.
solution-leakage.def: Solution leakage is contamination inside a single task: the answer, or a near-complete recipe for it, sits in the input the model is given. The canonical example comes from SWE-bench-style benchmarks built on real GitHub issues — some issue reports describe the exact fix, sometimes including the code, so "solving" the task means transcription rather than software engineering. It differs from training-data contamination in that no memorization is involved; the task itself is broken. It is one of the core reasons benchmark instances need manual auditing before their scores are trusted. See Case Study: SWE-bench.

canary-string.name: Canary string
canary-string.short: A unique marker token embedded in benchmark files so anyone can later check whether a model trained on them — if the model knows the string, the data leaked in.
canary-string.def: A canary string is a long, globally unique random identifier (a GUID) embedded in a benchmark's files, a convention popularized by BIG-bench. It serves two purposes: training-data pipelines can filter out any document containing the canary, keeping the benchmark out of training sets; and after the fact, anyone can probe a model for knowledge of the string — since it appears nowhere else on earth, recognition is proof the benchmark text entered training. Like its namesake in the coal mine, it detects the problem rather than preventing it: filtering only works if data pipelines actually look for it. See Defenses: Live Sets, Private Splits, Canaries.

private-holdout.name: Private holdout
private-holdout.short: A benchmark's secret test set, never published, so models can't have trained on it — scoring requires submitting to the benchmark's owners.
private-holdout.def: A private holdout defends a benchmark against contamination by simply never publishing part of the test data: a public split lets people develop and self-evaluate, while official scores come from a hidden split that only the benchmark maintainers can run (ARC-AGI is a well-known example of this design). What can't be downloaded can't be trained on or tuned against. The costs are real, though: scoring depends on the maintainers' availability and honesty, the community can't audit hidden tasks for errors, and every official evaluation risks leaking a bit — the model provider sees the tasks even if the public doesn't. See Defenses: Live Sets, Private Splits, Canaries.
private-holdout.also: private test set, hidden test set

live-benchmark.name: Live benchmark
live-benchmark.short: A benchmark that continually adds fresh test questions created after models' training cutoffs, so the current questions can't be in any model's training data.
live-benchmark.def: A live benchmark fights contamination with freshness: instead of a fixed test set that inevitably leaks onto the web, it regularly mints new questions — from recent competitive-programming contests, recent news, freshly generated puzzles — dated after every current model's training cutoff (LiveBench and LiveCodeBench are the namesake examples). A question that didn't exist when the training data was collected cannot have been memorized. The trade-offs: scores from different time windows aren't directly comparable, question quality must be maintained forever rather than audited once, and the approach only suits domains with a steady supply of fresh material. See Defenses: Live Sets, Private Splits, Canaries.

training-cutoff.name: Training cutoff
training-cutoff.short: The date after which a model saw no training data. Content created after the cutoff can't be memorized — the dividing line live benchmarks exploit.
training-cutoff.def: A model's training cutoff is the freshness boundary of its knowledge: the latest date represented in its training data. For evaluation it doubles as a contamination dividing line — any benchmark question created and published after a model's cutoff is provably absent from its training data, which is exactly the property live benchmarks are built on. Two caveats keep it from being a clean guarantee: vendors' stated cutoffs are approximate and data collection isn't a single sharp date, and models are often updated after release through fine-tuning that can introduce newer data.

n-gram-overlap.name: n-gram overlap
n-gram-overlap.short: A contamination check that searches for benchmark text appearing word-for-word (in chunks of n consecutive words) inside a training corpus.
n-gram-overlap.def: An n-gram is just a run of n consecutive words or tokens; n-gram overlap checks for contamination by scanning a training corpus for chunks that exactly match chunks of benchmark text. Long verbatim matches are strong evidence the benchmark leaked into training. It is the workhorse first-pass check because it's cheap and mechanical — but it only catches verbatim copying: paraphrased, translated, or reformatted versions of a test question slip through entirely, and running the check at all requires access to the training corpus, which outsiders rarely have. That is why it's complemented by behavioral probes like log-likelihood tests. See Data Contamination.

log-likelihood.name: Log-likelihood
log-likelihood.short: A score for how probable a model finds a given piece of text. Suspiciously high probability on benchmark text suggests the model saw it in training.
log-likelihood.def: A language model can assign a probability to any text — how likely it would be to produce exactly those tokens — and the log-likelihood is that probability on a logarithmic scale (logs turn the product of many tiny per-token probabilities into a manageable sum). Beyond its everyday roles in how models are trained and how some multiple-choice evals are scored, it serves as a contamination probe: text a model trained on tends to get conspicuously higher likelihood than fresh text of the same kind, so a model that finds one benchmark's exact phrasing unusually probable — especially compared to reworded versions — has likely seen it before. See Data Contamination.

saturation.name: Saturation
saturation.short: When top models all score near a benchmark's ceiling, leaving no headroom — the benchmark can no longer distinguish good models from better ones.
saturation.def: A benchmark saturates when frontier models approach its maximum score: once everyone is bunched near the ceiling, remaining differences are mostly noise, label errors, and ambiguous items rather than capability gaps, and the benchmark stops carrying information. Saturation is the natural life cycle of every successful benchmark — models improve, and the field's optimization pressure points straight at whatever is being measured — and it is frequently entangled with contamination, since an aging public benchmark has had years to leak into training data. A saturated benchmark isn't "solved" so much as retired: it gets replaced by a harder successor. See What Does a Score Mean?.

tracing.name: Tracing
tracing.short: Recording the full execution of an LLM application — every model call, tool call, and intermediate step with inputs, outputs, timing, and cost — for inspection and evaluation.
tracing.def: Tracing instruments an LLM application to capture everything that happened during a request: each model call's exact prompt and response, each tool invocation, each retrieval, with timings and token costs, organized into a tree of spans. It exists because LLM systems fail in ways logs of inputs and outputs alone can't explain — the bug is usually in an intermediate step (a mangled prompt, a bad retrieval, a misparsed tool result) that only the full trace reveals. Traces are also the raw material of the eval flywheel: error analysis reads them, and production traces become test cases. The term and tooling are borrowed from distributed-systems observability.

span.name: Span
span.short: One timed operation inside a trace — a single model call, tool call, or retrieval step, with its inputs, outputs, duration, and metadata.
span.def: A span is the unit a trace is built from: one named, timed operation — "call the model," "search the vector store," "run this tool" — recording its inputs, outputs, start and end times, and metadata like token counts. Spans nest: a request's root span contains child spans for each step, forming a tree that shows both what happened and what invoked what. The structure (inherited from distributed-tracing standards like OpenTelemetry) is what lets observability tools answer pointed questions — which step burned the latency, what exact prompt did the third model call receive — instead of presenting one undifferentiated blob. See Tracing and Online Evaluation.

observability.name: Observability
observability.short: The practice (and tooling) of being able to see what your LLM application is doing in production — traces, scores, costs, latencies — so you can find and fix failures.
observability.def: Observability is the ability to answer "what is my system actually doing, and why did this output happen?" from recorded evidence — traces, metrics, logs, and scores — rather than guesswork. For LLM applications it earns special attention because the systems are nondeterministic and fail silently: there is no stack trace for a confidently wrong answer, so without recorded traces and online evaluation scores you simply don't know how often production is failing or where. Platforms in this space (Langfuse, Braintrust, and others) combine trace capture with scoring and dataset curation, closing the loop between production behavior and offline evals. See Tracing and Online Evaluation.

assertion.name: Assertion
assertion.short: A simple programmatic check applied to an LLM output — contains this string, valid JSON, under this length, passes this regex — the cheapest kind of grader.
assertion.def: An assertion is a deterministic, code-based check on an output: does it contain the required phrase, parse as JSON, match a regex, stay under a length limit, avoid a forbidden term? Assertions are the cheapest and most trustworthy graders — instant, free, perfectly consistent — and tools like promptfoo organize entire eval suites around lists of them. Their limit is that they check surface properties: an answer can pass every assertion and still be wrong, unhelpful, or fabricated. The craft is decomposing quality into whatever is assertable and reserving expensive graders (humans, LLM judges) for what remains. See The Tooling Landscape.

solver.name: Solver
solver.short: In the Inspect harness, the component that produces a candidate answer for a task — anything from a single model call to a full multi-step agent.
solver.def: Solver is the term the Inspect eval framework (from the UK AI Safety Institute) uses for the "attempt the task" half of an eval: the pluggable component that takes a task's input and produces an answer, whether that means one prompt-and-respond call, a chain-of-thought recipe, or a tool-using agent loop running in a sandbox. Separating the solver from the scorer (which grades the result) is the framework's key design move: you can swap solving strategies while holding the grading fixed, or vice versa, and know exactly which change moved the score. See Inspect: A Harness in Depth.

scorer.name: Scorer
scorer.short: The component of an eval harness that grades a candidate answer — by exact match, code checks, or a model-graded judgment — producing the per-sample result.
scorer.def: A scorer is the grading half of an eval harness: it takes the output a solver produced (plus the target answer, if there is one) and emits a verdict — pass/fail, a numeric score, sometimes an explanation. Scorers range from trivial (exact match, includes) through programmatic (run the unit tests) to model-graded (an LLM judge applies a rubric). The term is Inspect's, but the role exists in every framework, and it is where an eval's validity concentrates: per-sample scores get aggregated into the metric, so a systematically wrong scorer corrupts everything downstream no matter how good the dataset is. See Inspect: A Harness in Depth and Validating the Grader.

epoch.name: Epoch
epoch.short: In eval harness terminology (Inspect), one of several repeated runs of the same sample — used to average out the randomness in model outputs.
epoch.def: In Inspect's terminology, an epoch is one complete pass over the eval's samples; running multiple epochs means attempting every sample several times. The reason is nondeterminism: a model generating with nonzero temperature can pass a sample on one try and fail it on the next, so a single attempt per sample tangles the model's ability up with per-run luck. Repeated trials let the harness both report a steadier average and compute reliability metrics — multiple attempts per task are exactly what pass@k and pass^k are computed from. (Unrelated to the ML-training sense of "epoch," one pass over training data.)

experiment.name: Experiment
experiment.short: In eval platforms (Braintrust usage), one recorded eval run — a system version scored against a dataset — stored so it can be diffed against other runs.
experiment.def: In eval-platform terminology (notably Braintrust's), an experiment is one tracked eval run: a particular version of your system (prompt, model, scaffold) executed against a dataset with scorers, with every output and score stored. The point is comparison over time — because experiments are persisted with their configuration, the platform can diff any two: which samples improved after the prompt change, which regressed, how the aggregate moved. This turns evaluation from a one-off score into regression testing for model behavior, where every proposed change gets an experiment and a diff before it ships. See Tracing and Online Evaluation.

faithfulness.name: Faithfulness
faithfulness.short: A RAG metric: is every claim in the generated answer actually supported by the retrieved documents? Low faithfulness means the model added things its sources don't say.
faithfulness.def: Faithfulness — one of the four core RAG metrics popularized by the Ragas framework — checks whether the generated answer sticks to its sources: each claim in the answer is extracted and verified against the retrieved context, and claims the context doesn't support count against the score. It targets the failure RAG exists to prevent: the model ignoring (or embellishing beyond) the documents it was handed and generating from its own parametric memory instead. Note what it doesn't check — an answer can be perfectly faithful to retrieved documents that were themselves wrong or irrelevant, which is why it's paired with the retrieval-side metrics context precision and context recall.

answer-relevancy.name: Answer relevancy
answer-relevancy.short: A RAG metric: does the generated answer actually address the question that was asked, rather than wandering off or answering something adjacent?
answer-relevancy.def: Answer relevancy — another of the four Ragas RAG metrics — measures whether the answer is on-topic for the question: complete answers to the question asked score high; evasive, rambling, or tangential responses score low. A common implementation inverts the problem: ask a model what question this answer would be answering, and compare that reconstruction to the question actually asked. It complements faithfulness, which alone is gameable — an answer faithfully grounded in the documents can still fail to address what the user wanted, and relevancy is the metric that catches it. See The Tooling Landscape.

context-precision.name: Context precision
context-precision.short: A RAG metric for the retrieval step: of the documents retrieved, how many were actually relevant to the question — and were the relevant ones ranked on top?
context-precision.def: Context precision evaluates the retrieval half of a RAG system: of the chunks the retriever fetched, what share are actually relevant to the question, with extra weight on the relevant ones being ranked first (since models attend most reliably to what appears early in context)? It is precision applied to retrieved documents. Low context precision means stuffing the prompt with off-topic material — which wastes the context window and actively invites the generator to ground its answer in the wrong text. Its partner metric, context recall, asks the opposite question: did anything necessary get missed? Both come from the Ragas family of RAG metrics.

context-recall.name: Context recall
context-recall.short: A RAG metric for the retrieval step: did the retrieved documents contain all the information needed to answer correctly, or did retrieval miss something essential?
context-recall.def: Context recall asks whether retrieval found everything needed: taking a reference answer as the standard, it checks how much of that answer's content is actually supported by the retrieved chunks. It is recall applied to retrieval, and it catches the silent RAG failure that generation-side metrics can't see: if the key document was never fetched, even a perfectly faithful generator must answer incompletely or refuse — and the trace looks fine unless you check what retrieval missed. Unlike its partner context precision, it typically needs a ground-truth reference answer to grade against. Part of the Ragas family of RAG metrics.

neuron.name: Neuron
neuron.short: A single unit inside one layer of a neural network; for every input token it produces one number, its activation.
neuron.def: In a transformer language model, a neuron is one unit of an MLP (feed-forward) layer. For every token the model processes, the neuron outputs a single number, its activation; most neurons sit near zero most of the time and rise on particular tokens or contexts. GPT-2 XL has 307,200 of them. Interpretability work tries to say in words when a neuron fires (a neuron explanation), and Module 8 is about how such a statement is tested. Many neurons respond to several unrelated things at once (polysemanticity), which is why some work explains learned directions called features instead.

activation.name: Activation
activation.short: The number a neuron (or feature) outputs for one token; the quantity an explanation of that neuron is supposed to predict.
activation.def: An activation is the value a neuron or feature produces on one token of one text. A neuron's activations across a text are the raw data of interpretability: an explanation such as 'fires on legal citations' is a prediction that activations will be high on citation tokens and near zero elsewhere. In simulation scoring, activations are normalized to a 0–10 integer scale (the neuron's largest value ever observed maps to 10, negatives to 0) so that a language model can read and predict them.

neuron-explanation.name: Neuron explanation
neuron-explanation.short: A natural-language description of when a neuron or feature fires; treated in this course as a hypothesis that predicts activations on unseen text.
neuron-explanation.def: A neuron explanation is a sentence like 'fires on four-digit years' that claims to describe a neuron's behavior. Usually it is written from the neuron's max-activating examples, which makes it a description of a handful of texts. Read as a claim about the neuron it is a hypothesis: it predicts an activation for every token of every text, and it is validated the way a grader is, on held-out data against ground truth. The two tests the course covers are simulation scoring (observational) and intervention (causal); see page 27.

simulation-scoring.name: Simulation scoring
simulation-scoring.short: Testing a neuron explanation by having a model predict the neuron's activations on held-out text from the explanation alone, then correlating the predictions with the real activations.
simulation-scoring.def: Simulation scoring (Bills et al. 2023) is the standard held-out test for a neuron explanation. An explainer model writes the explanation from example activations; a separate simulator model, shown only the explanation and new text excerpts, predicts an activation for every token; the score is the correlation between the simulated and real activations across those tokens, 1 for a perfect match and about 0 for an unrelated explanation. The score depends on the scoring set: 'top-and-random' mixes top-activating and random excerpts and is nearly blind to false positives, so a broad explanation can score well. Page 27 gives the method and its numbers; page 28 the controls it needs.

max-activating-examples.name: Max-activating examples
max-activating-examples.short: The texts on which a neuron fires hardest; the usual raw material for writing an explanation, and a biased sample of what the neuron does.
max-activating-examples.def: A neuron's max-activating examples (top examples, top dataset examples) are the excerpts, out of a large corpus, that produce its largest activations. Explanations are usually written by reading them, which is why they are a hazard: they show the neuron at its most certain and hide the long middle of its range, where a unit that looks single-purpose at the top may respond to other things. Scoring an explanation on the same examples that produced it is a training-set score. Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' sampled across eleven activation intervals instead; see page 28.

polysemanticity.name: Polysemanticity
polysemanticity.short: A neuron or unit responding to several unrelated things; the main reason one-sentence explanations of neurons score poorly, and something top examples alone cannot reveal.
polysemanticity.def: A unit is polysemantic when it fires on several unrelated kinds of input (the classic example is a vision neuron for both cat faces and car fronts). Bills et al. 2023 found the typical GPT-2 XL neuron 'appeared quite polysemantic', and Huang et al. 2023 measured the same thing as recall failures, neurons firing on strings their explanation did not cover. Because the secondary jobs rarely produce a neuron's very largest activations, an explanation written from max-activating examples cannot detect them; you have to sample across the activation range. Whether polysemanticity is pervasive in modern models is the subject of the 2026 dispute in page 29. Sparse autoencoders are one proposed remedy.

control-neuron.name: Control neuron
control-neuron.short: A randomly chosen neuron the explanation is not about, scored with the same explanation on the same held-out text; the baseline that gives an explanation score its scale.
control-neuron.def: A control neuron is the interpretability version of the control check from page 20: take the explanation and its simulated activations, but correlate them with the real activations of a random unit from the same layer. If the score barely drops, the score was measuring the text, not the neuron. Huang et al. 2023 used exactly this baseline (random pairings scored an F1 of zero against 0.56 for the real pairings). The same control applies to causal claims: ablate a random neuron and compare the behavioral effect. Page 28 works one by hand, alongside the shuffled-label control and a baseline explanation.

permutation-test.name: Permutation test
permutation-test.short: A hypothesis test that builds the null distribution by shuffling the labels (here, the real activations) and recomputing the statistic many times; the p-value is the fraction of shuffles that match or beat the observed value.
permutation-test.def: A permutation test asks how often a statistic would be as large as observed if the pairing between two lists carried no information. Shuffle one list (for an explanation score, the real activations across tokens), recompute the correlation, repeat thousands of times, and the fraction of shuffles at or above the observed score is a p-value under the null hypothesis of no relationship. It needs no distributional assumptions and is the shuffled-label control on page 28. It is the cousin of the bootstrap (Appendix F): the bootstrap resamples to estimate uncertainty, the permutation test reshuffles to test a null.

intervention.name: Intervention
intervention.short: Changing a unit's activation inside the running model (ablating it, or swapping in its value from another input) and measuring whether behavior changes; the test that separates a causal explanation from a correlational description.
intervention.def: An intervention edits the model's internal state and watches the output. Ablation sets a unit to zero or to its mean; an interchange intervention replaces its value with the value it took on a different input. Huang et al. 2023 read a neuron explanation as the causal claim that the neuron mediates the concept, and tested it with interchange interventions on tasks the model solves perfectly: GPT-4's explanations selected neurons with about the same causal effect as random selection. Bills et al. 2023 defined an 'ablation score' that substitutes simulated activations into the model and measures output divergence. A correlational score can be high while an interventional one is low; see page 28. It is the ablation probe of page 20 pointed inward.

sae-feature.name: Feature (SAE feature)
sae-feature.short: A learned direction in a model's activation space, found by a sparse autoencoder, intended to be more single-purpose than a raw neuron; explained and scored exactly as a neuron is.
sae-feature.def: A feature, in the sparse-autoencoder sense, is one of a large set of directions learned so that each activation vector is approximately a sparse sum of them. The hope is that features are monosemantic where neurons are polysemantic; Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' reported a median rubric score of 12 for feature intervals against 0 for neurons. For evaluation purposes a feature is a hypothesis like any other: it gets a explanation, a held-out simulation score, precision and recall, and the controls on page 28. Gao et al. 2024 add downstream loss, probe loss and ablation sparsity as feature-quality metrics.

sparse-autoencoder.name: Sparse autoencoder
sparse-autoencoder.short: A model trained to rewrite a layer's activations as a sparse combination of many learned directions (features), used to find more interpretable units than raw neurons.
sparse-autoencoder.def: A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is trained on a model's activations to reconstruct them through a wide bottleneck in which only a few units are active at a time; the units are the features. Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' (2023) applied one to a one-layer transformer; Gao et al. (2024) trained one with 16 million features on GPT-4 activations and introduced metrics for judging whether the features are any good, including explanation precision and recall. Reconstruction quality alone is not the goal, and Gao et al. warn that a baseline of zeroing the layer makes almost any reconstruction look excellent (98.2%). See page 28 and page 29.
